subject: math
title: Line Graphs: Scales, Trends and Reading Between Points
seo_title: Grade 6 Line Graphs Worksheets (BC Curriculum) – Free Math with Answer Key
meta_desc: Free Grade 6 math worksheets on line graphs for the BC curriculum: read scales, describe trends, estimate values between points, choose a line graph or a bar graph, and solve problems with Vancouver rainfall and temperatures. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: A line graph shows change over time. Check what one small square is worth before you read it.
key_sub: Up is an increase, down is a decrease and flat is no change. Between two readings, the line gives a good estimate. Use a bar graph, not a line, for categories like favourite sports.
body_html:
Read a line graph

A line graph shows how something changes over time. Time goes along the bottom. First check the scale: count the small squares between two labels and work out what one square is worth. Also check where the scale starts. It does not always start at 0.

To read a value, go up from the time to the dot, then across to the scale.

Example 1

What is the average high temperature in Victoria in October?

Go up from Oct to the dot. It is on the labelled line for 15.

Answer: 15 °C

Trends

A line going up shows an increase. A line going down shows a decrease. A flat line shows no change. The steepest part shows the biggest change. It is not always next to the highest point.

Example 2

Describe the trend from August to December. How much does the temperature fall?

The line goes down every month: 22, 20, 15, 10, 8. So it decreases. Fall = 22 − 8 = 14 °C.

Answer: It decreases by 14 °C

Read between points

When the data changes over time, like temperature or distance, the line between two dots gives a good estimate. Halfway in time is about halfway in value.

Example 3

Mei biked 2 km in 10 minutes and 4 km in 20 minutes. About how far had she biked after 15 minutes?

15 minutes is halfway between 10 and 20 minutes. Halfway between 2 km and 4 km is 3 km.

Answer: about 3 km

Line graph or bar graph?

Use a line graph for data that changes over time. Use a bar graph to compare separate categories, like favourite sports. Never join categories with a line: there is nothing between “hockey” and “lacrosse”.

DataBest graph
Height of a plant each weekLine graph
Rainfall in Vancouver each monthLine graph
Favourite sport of each studentBar graph
Students in each Grade 6 classBar graph

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Counting each small square as 1Work out the scale: 5 squares between 0 and 50 means 10 each
Reading the scale as if it starts at 0Check the first label: the scale may start at 5
Reading the wrong month or the wrong lineGo straight up from the month; use the key
Choosing the highest point for the biggest riseFind the steepest part and subtract
Using the nearest dot instead of reading between pointsHalfway in time is about halfway in value
Joining categories with a lineUse a bar graph for categories

faq.q: What do Grade 6 students learn about line graphs in BC?
faq.a: Line graphs are part of Data and probability in the BC Grade 6 math curriculum. Students read and make line graphs, describe trends, estimate values between points and decide when a line graph is the right choice.

faq.q: When should you use a line graph instead of a bar graph?
faq.a: Use a line graph when the data changes over time, such as temperature each month or the height of a plant each week. Use a bar graph to compare separate categories, such as favourite sports.

faq.q: What is a trend on a line graph?
faq.a: A trend is the general direction of the line. If it goes up, the data increases; if it goes down, it decreases; if it is flat, there is no change.

faq.q: Can you read values between the points on a line graph?
faq.a: Yes, when the data changes over time, like temperature or distance. Halfway between two times, the value is about halfway between the two readings, so it is an estimate.

sets.title: Read line graphs and their scales

items.q: What is each small square on the rainfall scale worth?
items.e: The labels go 0, 50, 100, 150, 200. There are 5 small squares between two labels. 50 ÷ 5 = 10, so each small square is 10 mm.

items.q: How much rain falls in Vancouver in an average October?
items.e: Go up from Oct to the dot, then across. It is 2 small squares above 100: 100 + 2 × 10 = 120 mm. (12 mm counts each square as 1 mm.)

items.q: In which month does Vancouver get the most rain?
items.e: The highest dot is above Nov: 190 mm. January (170 mm) and December (160 mm) are lower.

items.q: How much rain falls in an average February?
items.e: Go up from Feb to the dot. It is on the labelled line for 100, so 100 mm. (110 mm is March and 170 mm is January.)

items.q: Which month has an average of 90 mm of rain?
items.e: 90 mm is 1 small square below 100. The only dot there is above Apr. (March has 110 mm and May has 70 mm.)

items.q: How much rain falls in an average November?
items.e: The Nov dot is 1 small square below 200: 200 − 10 = 190 mm. (200 mm is the top of the scale, not a reading.)

items.q: What is each small square on the temperature scale worth?
items.e: The labels go up by 5. There are 5 small squares between two labels. 5 ÷ 5 = 1, so each square is 1 °C.

items.q: What is the average high temperature in Vancouver in July?
items.e: Go up from Jul to the dot. It is 2 small squares above 20: 20 + 2 = 22 °C. (20 °C and 25 °C are only the labels near it.)

items.q: Which month has the lowest average high temperature?
items.e: The lowest dot is above Dec: 6 °C. January is 7 °C and November is 9 °C.

items.q: What is the average high temperature in April?
items.e: The Apr dot is 3 small squares above 10: 10 + 3 = 13 °C. (3 °C forgets to start from 10.)

items.q: In which month is the average high temperature 9 °C?
items.e: Find 9 on the scale: 1 small square below 10. The dot on that line is above Nov. (February is 8 °C and March is 10 °C.)

items.q: What was the temperature at 6 a.m.?
items.e: The scale starts at 5, not 0. At 6 a.m. the dot is on the labelled line for 10, so 10 °C. (5 °C is the bottom of the scale.)

items.q: What was the temperature at 10 a.m.?
items.e: At 10 a.m. the dot is 2 small squares above 15: 15 + 2 = 17 °C. (12 °C counts 12 squares as if the scale started at 0, but it starts at 5.)

items.q: At which reading was it warmest?
items.e: The highest dot is above 2 p.m. (24 °C). At 4 p.m. it was 23 °C, a little cooler.

items.q: What was the temperature at 4 p.m.?
items.e: At 4 p.m. the dot is 2 small squares below 25: 25 − 2 = 23 °C. (18 °C counts squares from 0, but the scale starts at 5.)

items.q: What is each small square on the salmon scale worth?
items.e: The labels go up by 200. There are 2 small squares between two labels. 200 ÷ 2 = 100 salmon.

items.q: How many salmon were counted in week 3?
items.e: In week 3 the dot is halfway between the lines for 800 and 900. Halfway is 850 salmon.

items.q: In which week were the most salmon counted?
items.e: The highest dot is above week 4: 1200 salmon.

items.q: How many salmon were counted in week 1?
items.e: In week 1 the dot is halfway between 100 and 200, so 150 salmon.

items.q: In which week were 500 salmon counted?
items.e: 500 is halfway between 400 and 600. The dot there is above week 6. (Week 2 had 400 salmon.)

sets.title: Trends: increase, decrease and no change

items.q: Describe the trend in rainfall from March to July.
items.e: March 110 mm, April 90, May 70, June 50, July 40. The line goes down each month, so rainfall decreases.

items.q: Describe the trend in rainfall from August to November.
items.e: August 40 mm, September 50, October 120, November 190. The line goes up each month, so rainfall increases.

items.q: By how much does the rainfall increase from September to November?
items.e: September 50 mm, November 190 mm. 190 − 50 = 140 mm. (70 mm is only September to October.)

items.q: Between which two months does the rainfall decrease the most?
items.e: Find the steepest part going down. January to February: 170 − 100 = 70 mm. November to December is only 190 − 160 = 30 mm.

items.q: Between which two months does the rainfall stay the same?
items.e: A flat line shows no change. July and August both have 40 mm.

items.q: How does the rainfall change from February to March?
items.e: February 100 mm, March 110 mm. The line goes up 1 small square, and each square is 10 mm.

items.q: In which part of the year does the line go down?
items.e: From August (22 °C) the dots get lower each month until December (6 °C). Before July the line goes up.

items.q: By how much does the average high rise from January to July?
items.e: January 7 °C, July 22 °C. Rise = 22 − 7 = 15 °C. (6 is the number of months, not degrees.)

items.q: Between which two months does the average high fall the most?
items.e: September to October: 19 − 13 = 6 °C. October to November: 13 − 9 = 4 °C. November to December: 9 − 6 = 3 °C. The biggest fall is 6 °C.

items.q: Between which two months does the average high rise the most?
items.e: Find the steepest part going up. April to May: 17 − 13 = 4 °C. March to April: 3 °C. June to July: only 2 °C, even though July is near the top.

items.q: What does the flat part from July to August show?
items.e: A flat line means no change. July and August both have an average high of 22 °C.

items.q: Use the key. What is the average high in Kelowna in July?
items.e: Kelowna is the dashed line with squares. Each small square is 2 °C. In July its square is halfway between 28 and 30, so 29 °C. (22 °C is the Vancouver line.)

items.q: Which city has the bigger increase from January to July?
c: They increase by the same amount
items.e: Vancouver: 22 − 7 = 15 °C. Kelowna: 29 − 1 = 28 °C. Kelowna’s line is steeper.

items.q: In which month do the two cities have the same average high?
items.e: The two lines meet in October: both are 13 °C. In March, Vancouver is 10 °C and Kelowna is 9 °C.

items.q: How much warmer is Kelowna than Vancouver in July?
items.e: Kelowna 29 °C, Vancouver 22 °C. How much warmer means subtract: 29 − 22 = 7 °C.

items.q: In January, which city is warmer, and by how much?
items.e: Vancouver 7 °C, Kelowna 1 °C. 7 − 1 = 6 °C. (3 °C counts the 3 squares, but each square is 2 °C. 8 °C adds the two numbers.)

items.q: Describe the trend in the salmon count over the 7 weeks.
items.e: The count goes up from week 1 to week 4 (1200 salmon), then goes down to week 7.

items.q: Between which two weeks did the count go up the most?
items.e: Week 2 to 3: 850 − 400 = 450. Week 3 to 4: 1200 − 850 = 350. Week 1 to 2: 250. The steepest rise is week 2 to week 3, not the part that reaches the top.

items.q: By how much did the count go down from week 4 to week 7?
items.e: Week 4: 1200. Week 7: 200. 1200 − 200 = 1000 salmon. (300 is only week 6 to week 7.)

items.q: What does the flat part from 30 to 40 minutes show?
c: Mei biked back to the start
items.e: A flat line means the distance did not change. Mei stayed at 5 km for 10 minutes, so she stopped.

items.q: The temperature changed steadily between readings. What was it at about 9 a.m.?
items.e: 9 a.m. is halfway between 8 a.m. (13 °C) and 10 a.m. (17 °C). Halfway between 13 and 17 is 15 °C.

items.q: About what was the temperature at 11 a.m.?
items.e: 11 a.m. is halfway between 10 a.m. (17 °C) and 12 p.m. (21 °C). Halfway is 19 °C. (Do not just use the nearest dot.)

items.q: About what was the temperature at 5 p.m.?
items.e: 5 p.m. is halfway between 4 p.m. (23 °C) and 6 p.m. (19 °C). Halfway between 23 and 19 is 21 °C.

items.q: At about what time did the temperature reach 15 °C?
items.e: 15 °C is halfway between 13 °C (8 a.m.) and 17 °C (10 a.m.). So it was about halfway in time: 9 a.m.

items.q: After 2 p.m., at about what time was it 21 °C?
items.e: After 2 p.m. the line goes down from 23 °C (4 p.m.) to 19 °C (6 p.m.). 21 °C is halfway, at about 5 p.m. (It was also 21 °C at 12 p.m., but that is before 2 p.m.)

items.q: Why does it make sense to read this graph between the dots?
c: The temperature was measured every minute
The temperature keeps changing between readings
Any graph with a line can be read between dots
items.e: Time and temperature change smoothly, so there is a real temperature between two readings. The line gives a good estimate of it.

items.q: How far had Mei biked after 15 minutes?
items.e: 15 minutes is halfway between 10 minutes (2 km) and 20 minutes (4 km). Halfway is 3 km.

items.q: How far had Mei biked after 5 minutes?
items.e: 5 minutes is halfway between 0 minutes (0 km) and 10 minutes (2 km). Halfway is 1 km. (5 is the number of minutes, not kilometres.)

items.q: How far had Mei biked after 25 minutes?
items.e: 25 minutes is halfway between 20 minutes (4 km) and 30 minutes (5 km). Halfway between 4 and 5 is 4.5 km.

items.q: How far had Mei biked after 35 minutes?
items.e: From 30 to 40 minutes the line is flat at 5 km. Mei was resting, so at 35 minutes she had still biked 5 km.

items.q: How far had Mei biked after 45 minutes?
items.e: 45 minutes is halfway between 40 minutes (5 km) and 50 minutes (7 km). Halfway is 6 km.

items.q: At about what time had Mei biked 8 km?
items.e: 8 km is halfway between 7 km (50 minutes) and 9 km (60 minutes). So it was at about 55 minutes.

items.q: Mei kept biking at the same speed for 10 more minutes after 60 minutes. About how far would she be then?
items.e: From 40 to 60 minutes she biked 2 km every 10 minutes. 9 km + 2 km = 11 km. Extending the line is only an estimate.

items.q: At about what time had Mei biked half of the 9 km?
items.e: Half of 9 km is 4.5 km. 4.5 km is halfway between 4 km (20 minutes) and 5 km (30 minutes), so about 25 minutes. (30 minutes is half the time, not half the distance.)

items.q: About how tall was the plant on day 10?
items.e: Day 10 is halfway between day 8 (12 cm) and day 12 (20 cm). Halfway between 12 and 20 is 16 cm. (10 is the day, not the height.)

items.q: About how tall was the plant on day 14?
items.e: Day 14 is halfway between day 12 (20 cm) and day 16 (26 cm). Halfway is 23 cm.

items.q: About how tall was the plant on day 6?
items.e: Day 6 is halfway between day 4 (6 cm) and day 8 (12 cm). Halfway between 6 and 12 is 9 cm.

items.q: On about which day was the plant 28 cm tall?
items.e: 28 cm is halfway between 26 cm (day 16) and 30 cm (day 20). So it was about day 18.

items.q: About how much did the plant grow from day 10 to day 14?
items.e: Day 10: about 16 cm. Day 14: about 23 cm. 23 − 16 = 7 cm. (4 is the number of days.)

items.q: What is the best estimate of the temperature at 1 p.m.?
items.e: 1 p.m. is halfway between 12 p.m. (21 °C) and 2 p.m. (24 °C). Halfway between 21 and 24 is 22.5 °C.

items.q: Which graph is best to show the height of a sunflower every week for 8 weeks?
c: Line graph: it shows change over time
Bar graph: it shows change over time
items.e: The data is measured again and again over time, so a line graph shows how it changes.

items.q: Which graph is best to show the favourite sport of the students in your class?
c: Line graph: it shows change over time
Bar graph: it shows change over time
items.e: The data is in separate categories with nothing in between, so use a bar graph. Joining categories with a line makes no sense.

items.q: Which graph is best to show the temperature in Kamloops every hour for one day?
c: Line graph: it shows change over time
Bar graph: it shows change over time
items.e: The data is measured again and again over time, so a line graph shows how it changes.

items.q: Which graph is best to show the number of students in each Grade 6 class at your school?
c: Line graph: it shows change over time
Bar graph: it shows change over time
items.e: The data is in separate categories with nothing in between, so use a bar graph. Joining categories with a line makes no sense.

items.q: Which graph is best to show the number of salmon counted each day during a salmon run?
c: Line graph: it shows change over time
Bar graph: it shows change over time
items.e: The data is measured again and again over time, so a line graph shows how it changes.

items.q: Which graph is best to show how many cars of each colour are in the school parking lot?
c: Bar graph: it shows change over time
Line graph: it shows change over time
items.e: The data is in separate categories with nothing in between, so use a bar graph. Joining categories with a line makes no sense.

items.q: Which graph is best to show Ava’s mass on each birthday from age 6 to age 11?
c: Line graph: it shows change over time
Bar graph: it shows change over time
items.e: The data is measured again and again over time, so a line graph shows how it changes.

items.q: Which graph is best to show how many students walk, bike, take the bus or come by car to school?
c: Bar graph: it shows change over time
Line graph: it shows change over time
items.e: The data is in separate categories with nothing in between, so use a bar graph. Joining categories with a line makes no sense.

items.q: Which graph is best to show the average rainfall in Prince George each month of the year?
c: Bar graph: it shows change over time
Line graph: it shows change over time
items.e: The data is measured again and again over time, so a line graph shows how it changes.

items.q: Which graph is best to show the number of visitors to five BC parks last summer?
c: Line graph: it shows change over time
Bar graph: it shows change over time
items.e: The data is in separate categories with nothing in between, so use a bar graph. Joining categories with a line makes no sense.

items.q: Liam wants to show how many people joined his school’s Terry Fox Run each year from 2019 to 2026. Which graph shows the change best?
c: Bar graph: it shows change over time
Line graph: it shows change over time
items.e: The data is measured again and again over time, so a line graph shows how it changes.

items.q: Olivia measured the temperature of a cup of hot chocolate every 2 minutes as it cooled. Which graph is best?
c: Line graph: it shows change over time
Bar graph: it shows change over time
items.e: The data is measured again and again over time, so a line graph shows how it changes.

items.q: Kai showed his class’s favourite sports with this line graph. What is wrong with it?
c: The line should only go up
Sports are categories, so the dots should not be joined
items.e: A line shows change from one point to the next, like over time. Sports have no order and nothing in between them, so Kai should use a bar graph.

items.q: On Kai’s graph, the line between Hockey and Lacrosse passes 4.5. What does that point show?
c: Nothing: there is no sport between hockey and lacrosse
4.5 students chose a sport between them
The number of students who chose lacrosse
items.e: Between two categories there is no data, so a point on the line there means nothing. This is why categories are not joined with a line.

items.q: How many students in 6B chose soccer?
items.e: The soccer bar ends on the labelled line for 8, so 8 students. (4 counts the labelled lines, but each small square is 1 student.)

items.q: Why is a bar graph a better choice than a line graph for this data?
c: Each sport is a separate category
items.e: The sports are separate categories with nothing in between. Bars compare them; a line would suggest a change from one sport to the next.

items.q: Which data could be shown well on a line graph?
c: The colours of the bikes at school
The temperature at noon each day for a week
The number of pets of each kind in a class
The favourite fruit of each student
items.e: Temperature each day is measured over time, so a line graph shows how it changes. The others are categories.

items.q: Which data should NOT be shown on a line graph?
c: The rainfall in Nanaimo each week
The height of a cedar tree each year
Favourite ice cream flavours in Grade 6
The price of a bus pass each year
items.e: Ice cream flavours are categories with no order, so they belong on a bar graph. The others change over time.

items.q: Why does this graph use two lines and a key?
c: To show the total for both cities
To compare two cities over the same months
items.e: Each line shows one city over the same 12 months. The key tells you which line is which, so you can compare them month by month.

items.q: A line graph is the best choice when the data…
items.e: Line graphs show change over time, like temperature or height. For separate groups or favourites, use a bar graph.

sets.title: Word problems: Vancouver rainfall and temperatures

items.q: What is the total of the 12 monthly amounts on the graph?
items.e: 170 + 100 + 110 + 90 + 70 + 50 + 40 + 40 + 50 + 120 + 190 + 160 = 1190 mm. That is more than a metre of rain in a year. (1030 mm or 1020 mm leaves out a month.)

items.q: Spring Break is in March. How much more rain falls in an average March than in an average July?
items.e: March 110 mm, July 40 mm. How much more means subtract: 110 − 40 = 70 mm.

items.q: In how many months does Vancouver get more than 100 mm of rain?
items.e: Above 100 mm: January, March, October, November and December. That is 5 months. February has exactly 100 mm, which is not more than 100.

items.q: What is the ratio of July rainfall to November rainfall, in lowest terms?
items.e: July 40 mm, November 190 mm. 40:190. Divide both by 10: 4:19. July comes first, so it is 4:19, not 19:4.

items.q: What is the total rainfall for June, July and August?
items.e: 50 + 40 + 40 = 130 mm. (90 mm forgets June.)

items.q: A garden needs at least 80 mm of water a month. In how many months does rain alone give enough?
items.e: 80 mm or more: January, February, March, April, October, November and December. That is 7 months.

items.q: How much of the year’s rain falls from October to March?
items.e: October 120 + November 190 + December 160 + January 170 + February 100 + March 110 = 850 mm. Most of Vancouver’s rain falls in fall and winter. (680 mm leaves out January.)

items.q: Kai’s family drives from Vancouver to Kelowna in August. How much warmer is the average high in Kelowna?
items.e: Kelowna 28 °C, Vancouver 22 °C. 28 − 22 = 6 °C. (3 counts the squares; each square is 2 °C.)

items.q: In how many months is Kelowna’s average high 20 °C or more?
items.e: May 20 °C, June 24, July 29, August 28, September 22. That is 5 months. May counts, because 20 °C or more includes 20.

items.q: In how many months is Vancouver’s average high warmer than Kelowna’s?
items.e: Vancouver’s line is above in January, February, March, November and December: 5 months. In October the two are equal, so it does not count.

items.q: In which month is the difference between the two cities the greatest?
items.e: July: 29 − 22 = 7 °C. August: 6 °C. January: 6 °C. December: 6 °C. The lines are farthest apart in July.

items.q: Ji-woo’s family wants a picnic in Stanley Park in a month with an average high of at least 17 °C. Which months work?
items.e: May 17 °C, June 20, July 22, August 22, September 19. April (13 °C) and October (13 °C) are too cool.

items.q: How much warmer is the average high in August than in March?
items.e: August 22 °C, March 10 °C. 22 − 10 = 12 °C. (5 is the number of months, not degrees.)

items.q: Leah’s class started a hike at 8 a.m. and finished at 2 p.m. How much did the temperature rise?
items.e: 8 a.m. 13 °C, 2 p.m. 24 °C. 24 − 13 = 11 °C. (6 is the number of hours.)

items.q: The class wants to be off the trail before it gets warmer than 19 °C. By about what time should they finish?
items.e: 10 a.m. is 17 °C and 12 p.m. is 21 °C. 19 °C is halfway, at about 11 a.m. By 12 p.m. it is already 21 °C.

items.q: How many salmon were counted in all 7 weeks?
Simran says the salmon count doubled from week 1 to week 2. Is she right?
c: No: double 150 is 300, and the count was 400
items.e: Week 1: 150. Double 150 is 300. Week 2: 400, which is more than double.

items.q: Mei rested for part of her ride. For how many minutes was she moving?
items.e: The ride lasted 60 minutes. The flat part (30 to 40 minutes) is a 10-minute rest. 60 − 10 = 50 minutes.

items.q: While she was moving, in which 10 minutes did Mei bike the shortest distance?
items.e: 20 to 30 minutes: 5 − 4 = 1 km. The other moving parts are 2 km each. From 30 to 40 minutes she was resting, not moving.

items.q: Owen says July has 4 mm of rain, because the dot is 4 small squares above 0. What is his mistake?
c: Each square is 10 mm, so July has 40 mm
Each square is 5 mm, so July has 20 mm
He should count from the top: 160 mm
items.e: The labels go up by 50 with 5 squares between them, so each square is 10 mm. 4 × 10 = 40 mm.
